A common way to improve computer learning is to train many models and average their predictions [P3_p1_c02]. However, using a whole group of models together is cumbersome and can be too computationally expensive for a large number of users [P3_p1_c02]. 

The problem is that training needs to extract structure from massive datasets using huge amounts of computation, while serving many users has strict limits on speed and computing resources [P3_p1_c03]. 

To solve this, the paper uses a main idea called distillation [P3_p1_c03]. This transfers the knowledge from a cumbersome group of models into a single, smaller model that is much easier to deploy [P3_p1_c02][P3_p1_c03]. 

Regarding results, the paper shows surprising outcomes on MNIST and successfully improves a heavily used commercial speech recognition system [P3_p1_c02]. More than 80% of the accuracy improvement gained by a group of ten models is successfully transferred to the single distilled model [P3_p5_c02]. 

The paper also introduces specialist models to handle categories that full models often confuse [P3_p1_c02][P3_p6_c03]. These specialists can be trained rapidly and in parallel [P3_p1_c02]. 

As for limitations, when specialists are trained on heavily enriched data, they have a strong tendency to overfit on their special classes [P3_p8_c02]. The sources do not mention other limitations.
